cards.text: This song belongs to David, the shepherd who became king of Israel (1 Samuel 16:11-13; 2 Samuel 5:3). Its title ties it to the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, and the king drove him away. Getting run out of a room is rough, friend, and I say that as a stamper who got slid into the back of a junk drawer.

cards.question: In a song tied to a moment like that, what does David say he'll do at all times?

cards.text: David says his soul boasts in the LORD. Most bragging clears a room, but this is bragging about the LORD, and that's a whole different thing.

cards.question: David wants the ___ to hear his boasting in the LORD and rejoice.
David wants to praise the LORD on his own, with nobody else joining in.

cards.text: Then David tells his own story: "I sought the LORD, and He answered me". He reached out and the LORD answered, friend, which is more than I can say for any customer service line I have EVER called.

cards.question: David says the LORD delivered him from all his ___.
David says the faces of those who look to the LORD will end up covered in shame.

cards.text: Then David talks about "This poor man" who called out, and the LORD heard him. Baker, I came out of a closing-down bakery's bin with a 25 cent sticker on me, so I'm the poor man's POOR MAN.

cards.question: The LORD saved this poor man from just some of his troubles.

cards.text: Next, David says the angel of the LORD sets up camp, and he delivers. Meanwhile my whole security team in the junk drawer was a twist tie and the dead batteries I shared that drawer with.

cards.question: Where does David say the angel of the LORD encamps?

cards.text: Then David hands out an invitation, and he doesn't say hear about it. He says TASTE, and baker, I have been telling people that about cookies my WHOLE LIFE.

cards.question: David invites people to taste and see what about the LORD?

cards.text: David says blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him. Then he turns to the LORD's saints and tells them to fear Him.

cards.question: David tells the saints that those who fear the LORD lack ___.

cards.text: Then David brings in young lions. Strong, fast, built for the hunt, and if ANYBODY in this song should be set for life, it's them.

cards.question: What does David say happens to those young lions?
David says the young lions end up better off than those who seek the LORD.

cards.text: Now David switches hats and becomes the teacher. He says, "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD."
Then David asks who delights in life and wants to see good days. Friend, that's everybody who ever hit snooze hoping TODAY would finally be the good one.

cards.question: For anyone who wants good days, what's the first thing David tells them to do?

cards.text: David starts with the mouth, no evil and no deceitful speech, and friend, I have tried snatching a sent message back out of the air. You CAN'T.

cards.question: David says to sit back and wait for peace to come find you.

cards.text: Turn from evil, do good, chase peace down. Then David says the eyes of the LORD are on the righteous.

cards.question: The LORD's eyes are on the righteous, and David says His ears are inclined to their ___.

cards.text: But for those who do evil, David says the face of the LORD is against them.

cards.question: For those who do evil, what does David say happens to the memory of them?

cards.text: Then David says the righteous cry out, the LORD hears, and He delivers them from all their troubles. Sounds a lot like that poor man from earlier, doesn't it?

cards.question: David says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted.
David says the righteous won't face any afflictions at all.

cards.text: And for the righteous man, David says the LORD protects all his bones, and not one of them will be broken. Baker, I got carried across a kitchen and slid into the back of a junk drawer, and I would have LOVED that kind of coverage.
Then David turns to the wicked and says evil will slay them. And he's got a word for the haters of the righteous too.

cards.question: What does David say will happen to the haters of the righteous?
David ends the song with the LORD's servants: The LORD ___ His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned.

findings.problem: The right answer "Around those who fear Him" stands out. It is the only answer about people. The two wrong answers are places ("Beside the city gates", "On the holy mountain"). It also echoes the passage's own fear-of-the-LORD language, so a baker can spot it without reasoning.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The right answer "Keep your tongue from evil" sounds like Scripture. "Keep your guard up always" and "Keep your plans to yourself" read as modern everyday advice. The right answer stands out by tone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The comparison doesn't match the action. Verse 12 is about wanting life and good days. Hitting snooze is putting off the day, so "hit snooze hoping TODAY would finally be the good one" mixes two ideas and doesn't click right away.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The comparison doesn't match the action. Verse 20 is about the LORD protecting the righteous man's bones from being broken. Being carried across a kitchen and slid into a drawer involves no harm or breaking, so wanting "that kind of coverage" doesn't line up. The card also reuses the "slid into the back of a junk drawer" line from stop 1, card 1.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Verse 19 is only tested as "the righteous won't face any afflictions" (False). Its main point, that the LORD delivers him from them all, is never told on a story card or asked about. The baker can leave with only the afflictions half of the verse.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.
